speakerNotes.plainText: Have each person read one headline at a time; cluster only obvious duplicates. For any vague item, use the three prompts in order. “What went wrong?” keeps the statement outcome-based. “Because what?” moves toward a controllable condition without turning the session into solutioning. “How would we know?” creates an observable trigger. Keep the pace brisk: clarification should sharpen a risk, not litigate whether it is true. Park solutions in a separate area for later.

speakerNotes.plainText: Draw a simple two-by-two: likelihood left to right, impact bottom to top. Place each clustered risk by quick consent; do not score decimals or debate exact boundaries. If views differ, place the item at the more exposed position and flag the uncertainty. Then apply the forcing function: choose exactly three from the high-exposure region. Break ties by asking, “Which risk becomes cheaper if we act before launch?” The visual reveal numbers only three contacts, turning an unranked field into a decision.

speakerNotes.plainText: For each of the three risks, fill four fields. The risk is a concrete launch outcome. The owner is one accountable person—not a function or the whole team. The trigger is the earliest observable threshold that should cause action. The first action is small enough to start now. The owner does not personally solve everything; they keep the signal visible and convene the response. If assigning one row takes more than two minutes, the risk is still too broad: split or rewrite it.

manifest.title: Drever Basic
manifest.summary: A neutral visual baseline with generous space, clear typography, and focused motion.

principles: Give every slide one dominant idea
Use scale and space before decoration
Animate changes that clarify state or continuity
Prefer a meaningful visual over a longer list
avoid: More than two competing accent colors
Using a two-column layout when the ideas are unrelated

guidance: Use focus to keep prior evidence visible while making the current Step unmistakable.
Use replace for one changing state, compare for cumulative evidence, and stagger for at most four tightly related items.
Set flow to block for a vertical reading sequence and inline for a horizontal process or comparison; leave it unset when neither axis explains the content.
Basic uses mostly direct cuts and quiet fades; short spatial travel is exceptional and content remains more prominent than choreography.
Reuse a continuity name only when the same visual object persists across adjacent slides, then end the sequence as soon as it stops carrying the argument.

layouts.name: Cover
layouts.description: Open a presentation or major chapter with one concise title and restrained supporting context.

slots.name: eyebrow
slots.purpose: An optional short category, event, or chapter label.

slots.name: title
slots.purpose: The single dominant statement for the slide.

slots.name: supporting
slots.purpose: One short sentence that adds context without repeating the title.

slots.name: footer
slots.purpose: Optional speaker, organization, date, or section metadata.

layouts.example: <Cover eyebrow="Quarterly planning" title="Choose what happens next." supporting="The evidence, tradeoffs, and one decision the room can act on." tone="accent" />

layouts.name: TwoColumn
layouts.description: Place two related ideas side by side when their relationship is more important than either idea alone.

slots.name: primary
slots.purpose: The first argument, explanation, or visual group.

slots.name: secondary
slots.purpose: The comparison, consequence, or complementary visual group.
